after: ## 3.2.1 Types of non-adherence and why it matters
alt: Two cards show the types of non-adherence: failing to follow treatments (missed, wrong or early-stopped doses, ignored lifestyle advice) and failing to attend appointments. Below, the problems: for the patient, illness lasts longer or returns; for health services, wasted time and money and wrongly stronger prescriptions.
caption: Non-adherence harms both the patient and the health service.

after: ## 3.2.1 Types of non-adherence and why it matters
alt: Two columns contrast rational non-adherence, a reasoned decision after weighing side effects, cost, inconvenience and doubts, with unintentional non-adherence such as forgetting. Decision-based explanations fit the first but not the second, which needs prompts and routines. Notes summarise Laba et al. (2012) and the reductionism of the Health Belief Model.
caption: Decision-based explanations fit rational non-adherence, not forgetting.

alt: Three rows link a question to a measure: to find out why doses are missed, use an interview; how many are missed, an electronic dispenser; whether the drug has been taken, a blood or urine test. A note advises using two measures so each checks the other.
caption: Why: interview. How many: dispenser. Taken: biological test.

alt: A table lists five ways to improve adherence: the Funhaler for children, contracts, prompts, customising treatment and community interventions, with what each involves and the barrier it tackles, such as dislike of treatment, low commitment, forgetting or a regime that does not fit daily life.
caption: Pick the technique that targets the patient's barrier.

alt: Study card for Yokley and Glenwick (1984): aim, sample of 1,133 families and immunisation records as the measure; six randomly allocated conditions (four interventions, two controls); results ranking incentive, access, specific prompt and general prompt; the conclusion; and strengths and weaknesses.
caption: Specific prompts were the most cost-effective; incentives gave the biggest effect.

alt: Three columns, one per type of measure, each worth two marks: subjective interviews and the reasons they reveal, objective pill counts and electronic dispensers, and biological blood or urine tests that show recent use. A note gives the pattern of three types times two marks.
caption: Three types, each named with an example plus one detail, earn the six marks.
